It is impossible for any one to suggest any reason why Mr. Bryan should have been selected as the nominee of the convention if he had any regard to the views and conditions which have always heretofore prevailed on such occasions. The convention wanted to do something without knowing what, and it wanted to select some one to do that something, but it did not know who. Bryan delivered an impassioned stump speech with an actor's art while the convention was floundering around in this uncertain state, and everybody jumped up exclaiming that "he must be the man," because they did not understand what he was talking about, and supposed that it must, therefore, be something exceedingly wise.

The speeches Mr. Bryan has made since the nomination show that he has not grown at all. In one of his two speeches at Salem, Ill., on Wednesday, he said:

"Jefferson told us that the only duty of mankind was to protect men at the hands of their fellows. Every act beginning 'Thou shalt not' is simply an act intended to protect some individual from some other individual, and, my friends, I say to you that no government is worthy of the name which is not strong enough to protect its humblest citizen in every land from oppression."

If Jefferson had ever told us any such thing as that, he would not occupy the place in the regard of men that he does hold. Mr. Jefferson knew that man owes a duty to himself as well as to others, and whenever Mr. Jefferson said "thou shalt not" he intended every man to understand it as addressed to himself, in his own conduct, as well as to exhorting him to restrain another man from trespassing upon his neighbor. Mr. Jefferson intended him to understand the command to be "thou shalt not steal," "thou shalt not commit murder," "thou shalt not do anything which will incite thy fellow-man to breaches of the moral law," as well as commanding him to aid his fellow-man in holding on to that which is his.

Mr. Bryan does not seem to have the faintest conception of Jefferson's functions in respect to the first line of duty, and he seems to regard his advice to us to aid all men in preserving that which is theirs as countenanceing us to pay our dues by paying them in doubly-valued silver dollars. Mr. Bryan may be a rhetorician, but he is not very strong on logic.

This, however, is to be noted of Mr. Bryan's speech-making tour through Illinois. He has been exuberantly honored on that tour, but he has been compelled to share his honors everywhere with Altgeld. At Binghamton there were at least 100 people assembled to greet him, but the cries that went up were in equal proportions for "Bryan, free silver" and "Altgeld," and there were more cheers when Altgeld was called for than when either of the other cries was made.

In the placards advertising the meeting that was to be held in Mr. Bryan's honor at his old home, Salem, it was announced that Governor Altgeld would be there. We do not know, therefore, how much of the attention that has been shown Mr. Bryan in Illinois is attention to him and how much to his hacker, Altgeld.

Things then, have come to a pretty pass that the nominee of the Democratic party should be one who openly declared in Birmingham, Ill., in 1895, that he would bolt the Democratic nomination unless the candidate suited him, and that this nominee should be traversing the country making stump speeches to laud a platform composed in equal parts of anarchy and socialism, with Altgeld, the foremost of American anarchists, backstanding him and dividing honors with him. Surely something has happened that men know not of.

Madras of different qualities, but all cool and sheer, fancy muslins—the latter not so smart as the Madras ginghams—and thin weight of fancy white duck are used. The solid colors with a hair stripe of white, while not the newest, still rank among the most desirable patterns. The old-fashioned lowered chintzes that are associated in our minds with curtain hangings have been reproduced in the Madras shirtings. A pale pink and white square pattern will have sprays of tiny pink roses. Purple and white will have also pink, all in the dull colors used in old English goods. The accepted pattern for these shirts has a yoke at the back, with a little fullness directly in the center, which is held in at the belt by a stitched band that only extends to the side seams; from there a tape ties down the fullness in front. There is no yoke in the front of the shirt, but four narrow side pleats. The favorite pattern for sleeves is the bishop sleeve; but again in the Madras shirt this is very much modified, and shapes in at the hand into turned-over stiffened cuff of the material. The collars are made separate from the shirt, and are white, turned over, very much on the same cut as in years; but the neck of the shirt is so finished that stock can be worn just as well as collar. Stocks of this season are quite odd, and a novelty which will not be very popular, a straight band of satin or silk is fastened in the back, having very much the effect of clergyman's collar, and a black satin tie in a stiff bow in front finishes it off. Shirts made to order cost anything the makers choose to ask, but for stout people are desirable in so far that the careful fitting over the shoulders, and the equally careful arrangement of the fullness, produce much better results and longer lines.

In his earlier days Kelly was appearing at variety hall in San Francisco. The proprietor and manager of the place was German, who had a great admiration for the strolling man.

While Kelly was appearing at the theater the German arranged to put on the stage series of tableaux depicting the heroism of the members of the San Francisco fire department. Kelly was to stand at one side of the stage and recite some original verses describing each picture or tableau as it was shown on the stage. The German was wildly anxious that this tribute to the firemen should make a hit on the opening night.

"Oh, John," said, "do your best, and you will make the hit of your life!"

On the day of the opening Kelly remained at home, so as to be in the best possible trim for the show. Soon after 8 o'clock he started for the theater.

Just before going into the hall it occurred fun with the German; so he turned up his coat collar, unkempt his hair and went reeling into the variety hall.

There was a sound of crashing glassware. The German had dropped a tray full of beer glasses.

"Oh, John," he moaned, waving his hands in the air, "you have ruined all in front at that &c. to go to Irishmen to work for you!"

"That's all right," mumbled Kelly, staggering up to him.

"Go away!" shouted the manager. "You have ruined the show!"

With that the manager rushed for the stage and arranged that a soubrette should announce the tableaux. Then he went out in front and waited all in a tremble, to see if she could get through with it. In the meantime Kelly went around on the stage, and just as the soubrette walked on the stage Kelly followed her and said, "I'll take care of this."

The German saw him come on the stage, and with a cry of mortal terror ran for the front door. He knew that Kelly would spoil everything. He stood in the street, wiping his brow and in agony, when he began to hear loud applause inside the theater. He could hardly believe his senses.

touched and toned by the pressure of cor

selves and God, going to keep these vows

will fall by the wayside, but are the 9TH
crs going to help them on their feet again ::
Some will drift back into their habits in
spite of every moral and Christian influ-
ence about them. We are all familiar
with the parable of the sowing of good
seed, and we know that this parable
teaches the great truth that the growth

alone with their God.

prise all along the old and new lines. The
way these fields are cultivated, the man,
ner in which these great truths are hus-
banded and cultivated will decide the eter-
nal destiny of many Il man. woman and
child in this city.

Southwick of Albany permanent chairman. The secretaries were John S. Kenyon, Charles A. Ball, Lafayette Gleason and Reuben L. Fox.

It affirmed the principle of protection to American industries—a thorough and efficient protection, but yet a judicious one, not calculated to foster monopolies. It indorsed the principle of reciprocity.

Platt and Edward Lauterbach and to instruct the delegates to vote for McKinley if Governor Morton is not nominated on the first ballot. Remains of gold workings are found in many parts of that country, and even far in the southwestern part of Matabeleland remains which show that mining must have been carried on, by primitive methods no doubt, but still upon a scale larger than we can well deem within the capabilities of the Kafir tribes as we now see them. These old buildings are, with one exception, bits of wall enclosing forts or residences. They are constructed of small blocks of the granite of the country, carefully trimmed to one size, and are usually ornamented with simple pattern, such as the so-called "herringbone" pattern. The one exception is found in the ruins of Zimbabwe, in southern Mashonaland. Here a wall thirty feet high, and from six to twelve or fourteen feet thick, encloses a large elliptical space, filled with other buildings, some of which apparently were intended for the purposes of worship. There are no inscriptions of any kind, and few objects, except some rudely carved heads of birds, to supply any indication as to the chronology of the people who erected this building, or as to the nature of their worship. It would be possible for a man in Mr. Reed's position to make himself and his party offensive and thus send votes back to BRYAN and close up the ranks. The tone which he has adopted ought to be the tone of the Republican campaign throughout. If it is so, the happiest results may be expected. The sound money Democrats will go their own way, but none of them will be goaded to the support of Bryan by reason of anything done or said by the Republicans.

ANSWERED BY THE MINISTER OF WAR.

Paris Nov 15—In the Chamber of Deputies to-
day President Brisson gave the floor to General
Billot, Minister of War, when the proposed inter-
pellation of M. Casteln, Republican Revisionist,
in regard to the conviction of Captain Dreyfus, an
French military officer who was degraded and
sentenced to life imprisonment for betraying mil-
tary secrets to Germany, was called in its order.

General Billot read a short statement declaring
that the question was an extremely grave one, the
interests of Justice and the country being at stake.
The court martial which had tried and sentenced
Captain Dreyfus had been regularly constituted
and after an exhaustive examination of the case
had been unanimous in pronouncing judgment
against him. Later the Council of Revision had
given complete consideration to the case, and had
unanimously rejected Dreyfus's appeal from in-
judgment of the court martial, and nobody, Gen-
eral Billot said, had right to reopen the case.
Every precaution had been taken to prevent the
escape of Dreyfus from the Ile du Diable, on the
coast of French Guiana, where he is confined; he
urged no appealing to the patriotism of the Cham-
ber but to debate the question appropriately.

sion amid murmurs of dissent and demanded the
prosecution of the authors of the campaign in

broadcast the most infamous stories of Dreyfus
being the victim of a plot.

no fault in the Government and conviction that

casion to do so.

men and women on the globe, is extraordinary. The United States is among
the strongest nations of the world. It has the least reason of any great nation,
in mere sense to wish for arbitration. It is strong enough, in any but the most
absurd cause, to defend itself, to promote its policies and to carry on war, but its
very strength impels it to be backward.
It was pitiful, he said, that in
this time of peace, over nearly all the
world, more than a million men capable
of taking part in the progress of civili-
cation were kept under arms and billion dollars diverted to their support.
That time must come when the armies
of the world, like that of the United
States, would be a mere police body.
The force of public opinion must be as
constant as the law of gravitation for
solving the difficult problem of ending
war. The time would come when
armies, for aggressive purposes, would
be dissolved, and the angel of peace
would blow her trumpet over all the
world.


A letter from Chief Justice Fuller was
read, conveying the regret that his
health and public duties would prevent
him from testifying by his presence his
approval of the great cause of the con-
vention. Also a letter from Andrew
Carnegie, who referred to the move-
ment as "the noblest cause of this gen-
eration" and who, in postscript, men-
tioned the enclosure of a check for
$1,000 to help defray the expenses of
the meeting.


In the course of the general business,
Mr. John Doniphan of St. Joseph, Mo.,
created no little stir by moving that Mr.
Carnegie's gift be returned to him, be-
cause Mr. Carnegie had made his wealth
through contracts to furnish the gov-
ernment with munitions of war.


"And," he continued, "the press
charges him, whether justly or unjustly,
with making large profits by stinting
the employees in his work." He declared
that the boards of trade of the country
should pay the expenses of the meeting,
and that it will be humiliation to ac-
cept Mr. Carnegie's gift. The motion
was opposed by Delegate Weeks of
Pittsburg, editor of the Iron Manufac-
turer, and was buried under a large
majority.

attracted large audience. The speakers
were Hon. Carl Schurz, of New York,

sity and Edward Atkinson of Boston.

of the speakers in declaring that the United States should stand
ready to fight for honor and her terri-
tory. Each of the speakers at the night
session touched upon current questions.


President Angel said the practical diff-
iculties in establishing general court of
arbitration for several nations are very
serious, even if all the principal powers
are ready for it; but we have no evidence
that they are ready. It is, however, not
extravagant to hope that such course
may be set up by Great Britain and our
selves. Possibly we are more in danger
of drifting into war on slight occasions
than we were forty years ago. We have

its temptations and its dangers. One of
the great advantages of a compulsory re-
sort to arbitration is that time must be
gained for reflection.

now hardly large enough for the pow-

claims on other nations which are not
just claims. Let us show our confidence

bunal on all questions between us and
other powers which do not involve our
honor or our independence."
Mr. Schurz held arbitration to be prac-
tical, because eighty disputes had been
settled by that method in this country
and had stayed settled, while the result
of great wars had not stayed settled, but
had been subject to the shifting power.


Mr. Atkinson's speech was largely
a plea for the abolition of privateering.
Cities should be declared free from
bombardment and spoilation, making
such reservation for the defense of ha-
bors as would forbid the ships of an
petty state from interfering by force.
"Why," he asked, "should it be the
duty of officers of the navy to do what
would disgrace officers of the army?"
